question: Can I share my login credentials with a teammate who needs urgent access?
answer: No. Account sharing is strictly prohibited under Sec 2.2. Each employee must use their own credentials. Contact IT Service Desk for role-based delegation or temporary access.

question: Why should I use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
answer: MFA adds a critical second layer of defense. Even if an attacker steals your password, they cannot gain access without your second physical or biometric factor (Sec 2.3).

question: What should I do if I receive an unexpected MFA push notification on my phone?
answer: Deny the request immediately! Do not approve it. Repeated prompts indicate an MFA fatigue attack. Report it right away in NETRAK or call the Security Hotline.

question: Can I reuse my work password on external websites or personal tools?
answer: No. Reusing passwords across work and personal sites allows a breach at any external website to compromise your corporate identity (Sec 2.1).

question: Can I store my passwords in a text file or sticky note on my desktop?
answer: No. Passwords stored in plaintext are easily read by anyone near your desk or malware scanning your drive. Use the enterprise-approved password vault (Sec 2.1).

question: Is it safe to save corporate passwords in my web browser?
answer: Browser-stored passwords can be exported or extracted by malicious extensions and infostealers. Use the dedicated enterprise password manager instead (Sec 2.1 & Sec 5.4).

question: What should I do if an email asks for an urgent gift card purchase or wire transfer?
answer: Treat it as an executive impersonation attack (BEC). Never buy gift cards or initiate transfers without verbal verification via known phone numbers (Sec 3.2).

question: How do I check if an inbound email attachment or link is legitimate?
answer: Inspect the sender's full email domain (not just display name), look for spelling variations, avoid opening unexpected archives or macros, and report it if suspicious (Sec 3.2).

question: What are the common warning signs of a phishing email?
answer: Look for false urgency, generic greetings, mismatch between link text and destination URL, unexpected requests for passwords or financial actions, and spoofed domains (Sec 3.4).

question: I received an email stating my corporate account will be disabled unless I verify my password.
answer: This is a classic phishing lure. IT never asks you to verify your password via email links. Report the email immediately (Sec 3.4).

question: Someone called claiming to be from IT and asked for my one-time passcode (OTP). Should I provide it?
answer: Never! IT staff will never ask for your MFA code or password over phone, email, or chat. This is a vishing attempt (Sec 3.5).

question: Can I email company spreadsheets or documents to my personal Gmail to finish work at home?
answer: No. Sending company data to personal accounts violates Data Classification (Sec 4.1) and Cloud Storage (Sec 4.5) policies because personal inboxes lack corporate DLP protections.

question: Can I upload customer lists or databases to my personal Google Drive or Dropbox?
answer: Strictly prohibited. All corporate data must stay within the organization's approved tenant storage. Personal cloud accounts are unmonitored and violate customer NDAs (Sec 4.5).

question: Can I generate a public 'anyone with the link' share link for external contractors?
answer: No. Public links allow unrestricted anonymous indexing. You must share files directly to the contractor's authenticated email with an expiration date (Sec 4.3).

question: Can I paste company code or confidential reports into public ChatGPT or Claude?
answer: No. Pasting confidential data or internal code into public AI tools exposes proprietary information to third-party model retraining and log retention (Sec 9.1).

question: Can I install an AI browser extension or AI coding assistant on my work laptop?
answer: Only if it is listed in the Corporate App Catalog or explicitly approved by InfoSec. Unvetted extensions can read your active session tokens and confidential web pages (Sec 9.1 & Sec 5.3).

question: I found an unidentified USB flash drive in the office lobby. Can I plug it in to check the owner?
answer: Never plug in found USB drives. Attackers deliberately drop infected flash drives in lobbies. Hand it directly to Security or IT Reception for analysis (Sec 5.1).

question: Can I use my personal USB thumb drive to move files between my home PC and work laptop?
answer: No. Unencrypted personal USB devices can introduce malware or facilitate unauthorized data exfiltration. Endpoint ports are monitored (Sec 5.1).

question: Can I install a free online PDF converter or utility program from the internet?
answer: No. Online converters often retain uploaded files on third-party servers, and unvetted software installers may bundle adware or trojans. Use IT-approved tools (Sec 5.3).

question: Is it safe to work on company emails from airport or hotel public Wi-Fi?
answer: Public Wi-Fi is unencrypted and vulnerable to eavesdropping. You must connect to the corporate VPN before accessing any company email or internal resources (Sec 6.1).

question: Can my family members or children use my company laptop for homework or web browsing?
answer: No. Corporate hardware is strictly for authorized employee use. Non-employees can accidentally download malware or access sensitive files (Sec 6.3).

question: What should I do immediately if I clicked a suspicious link and entered my company password?
answer: Stop immediately. Disconnect from Wi-Fi/network, notify IT Security within 60 minutes, and reset your password from a clean device. Report the incident via NETRAK (Sec 1.2).

question: What should I do if my work laptop or phone is lost or stolen?
answer: Report it immediately to the Security Operations Center so they can trigger remote lock and wipe commands to prevent physical data extraction (Sec 1.2 & Sec 7.1).

question: Can I use my personal mobile phone to read work emails?
answer: Yes, provided the device enrolls in the corporate Mobile Device Management (MDM) profile, has a passcode, and is not jailbroken or rooted (Sec 7.1 & Sec 7.2).

question: Can I discuss confidential project roadmaps in coffee shops or open coworking spaces?
answer: No. Confidential information must not be discussed in public areas where competitors or strangers can easily overhear (Sec 4.2 & Sec 6.2).

question: Can I upload company source code to my personal public GitHub repository?
answer: Strictly prohibited. All company code belongs to the enterprise and must reside only in corporate private repositories (Sec 11.1).

question: What should I do if I accidentally commit an API key or password to a Git repository?
answer: Immediately revoke and rotate the secret, remove the commit from git history, and report the exposed credential to InfoSec via NETRAK (Sec 11.2).

question: Can I scan a QR code sent in an unexpected email to complete a verification step?
answer: Beware of 'quishing'. Attackers use QR codes to redirect you to phishing sites on your mobile phone, bypassing desktop security filters. Inspect the URL carefully (Sec 3.6).

question: Can I use WhatsApp or Telegram for quick work discussions with clients?
answer: No. Official business discussions must occur within approved corporate Slack or Microsoft Teams channels to ensure compliance, auditing, and data protection (Sec 4.4).

question: Can I grant third-party OAuth access to my Google or Microsoft work account for a free online calendar tool?
answer: Only if approved by IT Security. Rogue OAuth apps can silently read your entire calendar, email, and files without requiring your password (Sec 11.3).

question: Can I export customer records to an Excel file to test a script on my local computer?
answer: No. Exporting production customer records to personal environments creates major privacy and compliance violations. Use anonymized synthetic test data (Sec 8.2).

question: What is the Clean Desk standard?
answer: Clean Desk policy requires all physical documents, access cards, and removable media to be locked in secure cabinets whenever you leave your workspace unattended (Sec 10.1).

question: What should I do if someone follows me through the secure office door without badging in?
answer: Politely ask them to badge in at the reader or direct them to reception. Report unbadged individuals to building security immediately (Sec 10.1).

question: What precautions should I take when taking my company laptop on international travel?
answer: Notify IT Security 14 days before traveling. For high-risk regions, obtain a designated travel loaner laptop and leave your primary machine at home (Sec 6.5).

question: Can I throw printed papers containing internal notes into the normal office recycling bin?
answer: No. All documents containing business information must be placed into locked, secure shredding consoles for certified destruction (Sec 10.2).

question: Can I share a Miro or Figma whiteboard with external users without requiring logins?
answer: No. Whiteboards containing system designs or customer data must require authenticated logins. Never use anonymous public links (Sec 4.6).

question: Can I take screenshots of customer records or financial systems on my personal phone?
answer: No. Taking photos or screenshots of confidential company data on personal devices circumvents security logging and access controls (Sec 8.1 & Sec 4.1).

question: Can I install an unverified developer package or script from an unknown GitHub source?
answer: Developer packages must be checked for typosquatting, verified against trusted package registries, and vetted by automated scanning tools before installation (Sec 11.1).

question: Can I use private browsing (Incognito) mode to bypass company web safety filters?
answer: No. Incognito mode only prevents local history saving; it does not encrypt your traffic or bypass enterprise security monitoring (Sec 5.4).

question: Can I keep old customer files on my laptop indefinitely in case I need them later?
answer: No. Corporate Data Retention standards mandate regular purging of obsolete data to comply with privacy regulations and limit data breach exposure (Sec 8.3).
